questions.q: State three key properties of a normal distribution's shape.
questions.answer: A normal distribution is: (1) symmetric and bell-shaped, centered at its mean; (2) unimodal (a single peak at the mean); (3) its total area under the curve equals $1$, and it never touches the horizontal axis (it extends infinitely in both directions, getting closer and closer to zero).

questions.q: Explain what the two parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ control in a normal distribution's shape.
questions.answer: $\mu$ (the mean) controls the location of the center of the distribution (where the peak is). $\sigma$ (the standard deviation) controls the spread: a larger $\sigma$ produces a wider, flatter curve, while a smaller $\sigma$ produces a narrower, taller curve — but both remain symmetric and bell-shaped.

questions.q: Adult male heights are approximately normal with mean $70$ inches and standard deviation $3$ inches. Using the 68-95-99.7 rule, find the range of heights containing the middle 95% of adult men.
questions.answer: The 95% range spans $\mu\pm2\sigma=70\pm2(3)=70\pm6$, so from $64$ to $76$ inches.

questions.q: Using the same distribution, find the approximate percentage of adult men taller than $76$ inches.
questions.answer: $76$ inches is $\mu+2\sigma$. By the 68-95-99.7 rule, $95\%$ of the data lies within $2$ standard deviations, leaving $5\%$ split evenly in the two tails: $2.5\%$ above $76$ inches and $2.5\%$ below $64$ inches.

sections.heading: Standardizing and using the normal distribution

questions.q: Using the same height distribution (mean $70$, standard deviation $3$), find the $z$-score for a height of $77.5$ inches, and use a standard normal table value of $P(Z<2.5)\approx0.9938$ to find the proportion of men shorter than $77.5$ inches.
questions.answer: $z=\dfrac{77.5-70}{3}=\dfrac{7.5}{3}=2.5$. $P(X<77.5)=P(Z<2.5)\approx0.9938$, or about $99.38\%$ of men are shorter than $77.5$ inches.

questions.q: Find the proportion of men between $65$ and $75$ inches tall, given $P(Z<1.67)\approx0.9525$ and $P(Z<-1.67)\approx0.0475$.
The graph shows the standard normal distribution ($\mu=0$, $\sigma=1$), with the area to the left of $z=1$ shaded (though shading itself is not shown, imagine it visually).
parts: Using $P(Z<1)\approx0.8413$, find the area under the curve to the right of $z=1$.
Explain, using the curve's symmetry, why $P(Z<-1)=P(Z>1)$.
answers: The standard normal curve is symmetric about $z=0$. By symmetry, the area to the left of $-1$ is a mirror image of the area to the right of $1$, so $P(Z<-1)$ and $P(Z>1)$ must be equal.

sections.heading: Working backward: finding values from percentiles

questions.q: SAT scores are approximately normal with mean $1050$ and standard deviation $150$. A student scores at the $90$th percentile, corresponding to $z\approx1.28$. Find that student's approximate score.
Using the same distribution, find the score that separates the bottom $10\%$ of scores, given that $z\approx-1.28$ corresponds to the 10th percentile.
Explain how a normal probability plot (or normal quantile plot) can be used to assess whether a data set is approximately normal, and what a roughly straight-line pattern indicates.
questions.answer: A normal probability plot compares the ordered data values to what would be expected if the data were exactly normal. If the plotted points fall close to a straight line, the data is approximately normal. Systematic curvature or bending away from a straight line (such as an S-shape or clear bends at the ends) suggests the data deviates from normality — for example, skewness or heavy tails.

sections.heading: Applying the normal distribution to real data

questions.q: Pregnancy lengths are approximately normal with mean $\mu=266$ days and standard deviation $\sigma=16$ days. Find the $z$-score for a pregnancy lasting $250$ days.
Using the same pregnancy-length distribution and the 68-95-99.7 rule, find the approximate percentage of pregnancies lasting between $234$ and $298$ days.
questions.answer: $234=266-32=\mu-2\sigma$ and $298=266+32=\mu+2\sigma$, so this range spans $\mu\pm2\sigma$. By the 68-95-99.7 rule, approximately $95\%$ of pregnancies fall in this range.

sections.heading: Combining two independent normal random variables

questions.q: A vending machine dispenses a soda whose volume is normally distributed with mean $355$ mL and standard deviation $4$ mL, independently of a snack bag whose weight is normally distributed with mean $50$ g and standard deviation $2$ g. If $T$ represents the combined "total" formed by adding the soda volume (in mL) and snack weight (in g) as a single number, find the mean of $T$. (This is a simplified illustrative combination, not a real physical unit.)
questions.answer: For independent normal random variables, means add directly: $\mu_T=355+50=405$.

questions.q: Battery lifespans are normally distributed with mean $500$ hours and standard deviation $40$ hours. Find the $z$-score for a battery lasting $460$ hours, and describe its relative position.
questions.answer: $z=\dfrac{460-500}{40}=\dfrac{-40}{40}=-1$. This battery's lifespan is exactly one standard deviation below the mean.

questions.q: A company manufactures resistors with resistance values approximately normal, mean $100$ ohms and standard deviation $5$ ohms. A resistor is considered defective if its resistance is below $90$ ohms or above $110$ ohms. Using the 68-95-99.7 rule, estimate the percentage of resistors that are defective, and explain your reasoning step by step.
questions.answer: $90=100-2(5)=\mu-2\sigma$ and $110=100+2(5)=\mu+2\sigma$, so the acceptable range spans $\mu\pm2\sigma$. By the 68-95-99.7 rule, approximately $95\%$ of resistors fall within this range (not defective), leaving approximately $5\%$ defective (split as roughly $2.5\%$ below $90$ ohms and $2.5\%$ above $110$ ohms).

questions.q: Two students are comparing their standardized test scores from different tests. Student X scored 78 on a test with mean 70 and standard deviation 8. Student Y scored 165 on a different test with mean 150 and standard deviation 12. Using $z$-scores, determine who performed relatively better compared to their own test's distribution of test-takers, showing full reasoning.
questions.answer: Student X: $z=\dfrac{78-70}{8}=\dfrac{8}{8}=1$. Student Y: $z=\dfrac{165-150}{12}=\dfrac{15}{12}=1.25$. Since $1.25>1$, Student Y performed relatively better compared to their own test's distribution of test-takers, even though the raw score gap looks different for each test.
